questions.question: What makes an object eligible for garbage collection on ART?
options: Its reference count drops to zero
It has not been accessed for several GC cycles
The method that created it has returned
No chain of strong references from any GC root reaches it
questions.explanation: ART uses tracing collection: anything not reachable from roots such as thread stacks, static fields and JNI global references is garbage. It does not use reference counting, so cycles of unreachable objects are still collected, and leaving the creating method only matters if nothing else holds the object.

questions.question: ART's default concurrent copying collector stops all app threads for the whole time a collection runs.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Most of the work, including marking and copying, happens concurrently while app threads keep running; only short pauses are needed (for example to flip thread roots). Long stop-the-world collections were a Dalvik-era problem.

questions.question: Logcat shows GC messages several times a second while a list is scrolling. What is the most likely cause?
options: Too many short-lived objects allocated in hot paths like `onDraw` or `onBindViewHolder`
The heap limit is set too high by `largeHeap`
RecyclerView recycling its view holders
A memory leak keeping old activities alive
questions.explanation: Frequent collections during an interaction mean a high allocation rate: creating Paints, lists, strings or boxed values per frame or per bind. A leak shows up as a heap that keeps growing rather than as constant collections, and recycling view holders actually reduces allocations.

questions.question: Why does making the collector generational make GC cheaper for a typical Android app?
options: Most objects die young, so frequent collections of recently allocated memory free a lot while touching little
It moves old objects to native memory where they do not count toward the heap limit
It lets the app choose which objects to collect with annotations
It never has to scan old objects again once they are promoted
questions.explanation: The generational hypothesis says most allocations are short-lived, so collecting only young objects reclaims most garbage cheaply. Old objects still need occasional full collections and references from old to young objects must be tracked; nothing is moved out of the managed heap.

questions.question: The concurrent copying collector moves objects while app threads are running. What mechanism makes that safe?
options: Objects are never moved while any thread is running, only during app idle time
A read barrier on reference loads makes threads see the moved copy of an object
The app is paused while every pointer in the heap is rewritten
Every write of a primitive field is blocked until copying finishes
questions.explanation: Concurrent copying uses read barriers: when a thread loads a reference, the barrier ensures it gets the to-space copy if the object has moved. This adds a small cost to reference reads but avoids a long pause to fix every pointer. Primitive writes need no special handling for moving.

questions.question: Which of these act as GC roots that keep objects alive? Select all that apply.
options: Local variables in frames of running threads
Keys in a `WeakHashMap` that nothing else points to
Static fields of loaded classes
Objects referenced only by a `WeakReference`
JNI global references held by native code
questions.explanation: Static fields, live stack frames and JNI global references are all roots, which is why statics and long-running threads are classic leak sources. Weak references by design do not keep their referent alive, and a `WeakHashMap` drops entries whose keys are only weakly reachable.

questions.question: Calling `System.gc()` before a heavy screen is a good way to guarantee no GC will run during its animations.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: `System.gc()` is only a request, and even a full collection does not stop new allocations from triggering another one moments later. It also costs CPU at the wrong time; the real fix is reducing allocations during the animation.

questions.question: A Perfetto trace shows the main thread blocked in a slice like `WaitForGcToComplete` during a dropped frame, while `HeapTaskDaemon` is busy. What is the most likely cause?
options: The main thread is allocating faster than the concurrent GC can free, so an allocation had to wait for GC
A leaked Activity is making each GC slower
The RenderThread is holding the heap lock while uploading textures
A finalizer on the main thread threw an exception
questions.explanation: When the heap fills up during a concurrent cycle, an allocating thread must wait for the collector to free space, and the main thread shows up blocked on GC. The fix is to cut the allocation rate in that code path. Leaks raise heap occupancy but the immediate symptom here is an allocation stall, not a lock held by RenderThread.

questions.question: You need to find which code allocates the most objects while a screen scrolls. Which tools help? Select all that apply.
options: Android Studio Memory Profiler's Java/Kotlin allocation recording
Perfetto heap profiling (heapprofd) for native allocations
JankStats frame reports
LeakCanary's heap analysis
questions.explanation: Allocation recording and heapprofd capture allocation call stacks, which is what you need to find churn. LeakCanary reports objects that stay retained after they should be gone, not short-lived allocations, and JankStats tells you which frames were slow but not why.

questions.question: A class overrides `finalize()` to free a native handle. Under load, users see crashes with a `TimeoutException` mentioning `finalize()`. What is going on?
options: Finalizers run on a single daemon thread; a slow one exceeds the watchdog timeout and the runtime crashes the app
`finalize()` is not supported on ART, so the call threw immediately
The native handle was freed twice because ART runs each finalizer twice
Finalizers run on the main thread and triggered an ANR
questions.explanation: Finalizable objects are queued and run one by one on a finalizer daemon, and a watchdog kills the process if one takes too long. They also delay memory reclamation because the object survives an extra GC. Explicit `close()` or a `Cleaner`-style approach is preferred; finalizers do not run on the main thread or twice.
